# Canonical

> Canonical, the publisher of Ubuntu, provides open source security, support and services. Our portfolio covers critical systems, from the smallest devices to the largest clouds, from the kernel to containers, from databases to AI. With customers that include top tech brands, emerging startups, governments and home users, Canonical delivers trusted open source for everyone. Learn more at canonical.com.

---

## Company

### About Canonical

Canonical is the company behind Ubuntu and a provider of open source security, support and services. It provides commercial open source solutions across infrastructure, databases, AI, and IoT. Canonical publishes and maintains Ubuntu, develops the products built around it, and offers Ubuntu Pro subscriptions for long-term security, compliance, and support. To learn more about Canonical's full product portfolio, visit canonical.com.

Source: https://canonical.com/company

---

## Ubuntu OS

### Ubuntu Desktop

Ubuntu Desktop is a free, open source Linux operating system designed for elegance, security, and customizability. It provides a polished, intuitive desktop experience for developers, organizations, and everyday users, with built-in productivity tools including LibreOffice, Thunderbird, and the Firefox browser, alongside access to thousands of applications through the Snap Store.

New releases of Ubuntu Desktop come out every six months, with LTS versions every two years receiving five years of free security updates, extendable to up to 15 years with Ubuntu Pro.

Key features include native support for development toolchains (Python, Rust, Go, Node.js, Java, C/C++), container and VM support via Multipass, GPU acceleration for AI/ML workloads with NVIDIA CUDA and ROCm, Active Directory integration for enterprise fleet management via ADSys, and accessibility tools. Ubuntu Desktop is certified on hardware from vendors including Dell, HP, and Lenovo, with preinstalled options available.

### Ubuntu Server

Ubuntu Server is the most widely deployed Linux distribution for cloud and data center workloads. It combines developer familiarity with enterprise reliability, making it the natural choice for hosting web applications, databases, container platforms, private clouds, and enterprise services at scale.

Ubuntu Server is available for x86-64 and ARM64 architectures. LTS releases receive five years of free security updates, extendable to up to 15 years with Ubuntu Pro.

Ubuntu Server includes support for KVM virtualization, LXD containers, ZFS and Btrfs file systems, and automated provisioning via cloud-init, MAAS, and Landscape. It is the reference operating system for OpenStack and is certified on server hardware from vendors including Dell, HP Enterprise, Lenovo, and Supermicro.

### Ubuntu on WSL

Ubuntu on WSL provides a full Ubuntu terminal and toolchain within Windows. Ubuntu is the default distribution for Windows Subsystem for Linux, enabling developers to run Linux command-line tools, utilities, and applications alongside their Windows environment without the overhead of a traditional virtual machine. It supports the same package repositories and development tools as a native Ubuntu installation, and integrates with VS Code, Docker Desktop, and GPU passthrough for CUDA workloads.

### Ubuntu Core

Ubuntu Core is an immutable, fully containerized Ubuntu distribution designed for IoT, embedded, and edge devices. It is built for developers and device manufacturers who need a locked-down, security-hardened OS for devices deployed in the field, from industrial gateways and digital signage to networking equipment and robotics.

Every component of Ubuntu Core, including the kernel and OS itself, is packaged as a snap, providing strict confinement, transactional over-the-air (OTA) updates, automatic rollback on failure, and hardware-rooted secure boot via full disk encryption and TPM 2.0. Ubuntu Core supports x86-64 and ARM (armhf and arm64) architectures.

Device manufacturers can build custom Ubuntu Core images using the snapcraft toolchain, define a model assertion that pins the exact set of snaps and their update channels, and distribute updates through the Snap Store or an Enterprise Store.

### Snaps and the Snap Store

Snaps are universal Linux packages designed for security, portability, and consistency. Each snap runs in strict confinement using AppArmor and seccomp, isolating it from the host system and other applications. Snaps are cross-distribution compatible, running on Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, Arch, and other Linux distributions without repackaging.

Snapcraft is the build tool for creating snaps. The public Snap Store hosts thousands of applications and is the primary software distribution channel for both Ubuntu Desktop and Ubuntu Core devices. Enterprise customers can use the Enterprise Store to host and control snap distribution within their organization.

Source: https://snapcraft.io

### Multipass

Multipass is a command-line tool for launching and managing Ubuntu virtual machines on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It uses the native hypervisor on each platform (Hyper-V on Windows, HyperKit/QEMU on macOS, QEMU/KVM on Linux) and supports cloud-init for automated VM configuration. Multipass provides a consistent Ubuntu development environment across operating systems without the overhead of full virtualization management.

Source: https://canonical.com/multipass

---

## Infrastructure

### LXD

LXD is Canonical's open source container and virtual machine manager, used for running lightweight virtualized workloads, building development environments, creating multi-tenant hosting platforms, and providing compute isolation for edge and IoT deployments. Originally developed as part of the LXC (Linux Containers) project, LXD extends the LXC experience with a modern REST API, clustering, and unified management of both system containers and virtual machines. Since 2023, LXD has been fully maintained by Canonical under its own project governance.

LXD provides a unified experience for running system containers and VMs on a single host or across a cluster, managed via CLI, REST API, or web UI. Key features include live migration, snapshot and restore, storage pool management (ZFS, Btrfs, LVM, Ceph), network management (bridges, OVN, SR-IOV), image servers for preconfigured OS images, and project-based multi-tenancy.

Source: https://canonical.com/lxd

### OpenStack

Canonical OpenStack is an enterprise distribution of OpenStack for building and operating private clouds. OpenStack is an open source cloud computing platform that provides infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), enabling organizations to run virtualized compute, storage, and networking resources in their own data centers with cloud-like automation and self-service.

Canonical OpenStack is deployed and managed using Juju and charms, which automate day-0 through day-2 tasks including deployment, configuration, upgrades, scaling, backup, and integration. It integrates with the wider Canonical ecosystem including storage, networking, bare metal provisioning, and orchestration tools.

Canonical offers OpenStack consulting and deployment services at a fixed price, including architecture design, hardware procurement guidance, deployment, and workload migration. Ongoing support is available through Ubuntu Pro + Support, and fully managed OpenStack is available as a service with SLA-backed uptime guarantees.

Source: https://canonical.com/openstack

### MAAS (Metal as a Service)

MAAS is Canonical's bare metal provisioning tool. It gives data center operators the ability to treat physical servers like cloud instances, discovering, testing, commissioning, and deploying operating systems to bare metal hardware on demand, with full network configuration and lifecycle management.

MAAS automates the entire provisioning workflow from power-on to production-ready, eliminating manual server setup and enabling infrastructure-as-code workflows. It integrates with Juju for application orchestration on top of provisioned hardware. MAAS is open source and free to use, with commercial support available through Ubuntu Pro.

Source: https://canonical.com/maas

### Ceph

Canonical Ceph is an enterprise-supported distribution of Ceph, the open source software-defined storage platform. It provides block, object, and file storage through a unified cluster, and integrates with OpenStack, Kubernetes, and standalone deployments.

Canonical provides up to 15 years of security maintenance for Ceph, along with 24/7 support, consulting, and fully managed Ceph as a service. Deployment and lifecycle management are automated via Juju charms.

Source: https://canonical.com/ceph

### MicroCloud

MicroCloud is a lightweight, automated private cloud solution from Canonical that can be stood up in minutes. It combines LXD (compute), Ceph (distributed storage), and OVN (software-defined networking) into a single integrated deployment.

MicroCloud is designed for edge and distributed clouds, development environments, and lean cloud operations that are designed to be straightforward and low maintenance. It scales from three nodes upward, supports both virtual machines and system containers, and provides automated high availability and distributed storage out of the box.

Source: https://canonical.com/microcloud

### Juju

Juju is Canonical's open source orchestration engine for deploying, integrating, and managing applications on any infrastructure. It supports deployment targets including bare metal (via MAAS), public clouds (AWS, Azure, GCP), OpenStack, Kubernetes, LXD, and MicroCloud.

Juju uses charms to automate application lifecycle management. Charms are described in detail in the following section.

JAAS (Juju as a Service) provides a centralized dashboard for managing Juju controllers, models, and application topologies across multiple clouds with audit logging and RBAC.

Source: https://canonical.com/juju

### Charms

Charms are reusable software operators that encode operational best practices for deploying and managing applications. Each charm encapsulates the knowledge needed to install, configure, scale, upgrade, back up, and integrate a piece of software, replacing custom scripts and runbooks with a standardized, repeatable automation layer.

When two charms are related (for example, a database charm and an application charm), they automatically negotiate configuration, credentials, and connectivity. This relation-driven model means that adding a new component to a deployment, such as connecting a monitoring stack to an application, requires a single command rather than manual configuration on both sides.

Charms are published on Charmhub, an open marketplace of community and Canonical-maintained operators covering databases, observability tools, identity providers, networking components, and more. Canonical maintains charms for all of its major products, ensuring consistent operational quality across the stack.

Source: https://charmhub.io

---

## Public cloud

### Ubuntu on public clouds

Ubuntu is the most widely used operating system on major public clouds, including AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud, and Oracle Cloud. Canonical publishes optimized Ubuntu images for each cloud, tuned for the cloud's hypervisor and hardware, and certified by both Canonical and the cloud provider.

Ubuntu Pro is available on all major clouds, adding security patching for packages from the wider open source ecosystem, kernel Livepatch, FIPS 140 certified cryptographic modules, and CIS hardening profiles. Ubuntu Pro can be activated on any Ubuntu instance, either by launching a Pro-enabled image from the cloud marketplace or by attaching an existing Ubuntu instance using the `pro attach` command with a subscription token.

Canonical provides 24/7 support for Ubuntu workloads running on public clouds through the Ubuntu Pro + Support subscription.

---

## Security and support

### Ubuntu Pro

Ubuntu Pro is Canonical's comprehensive subscription for open source security, support and compliance. It extends Ubuntu LTS security maintenance from 5 to up to 15 years (with the Legacy add-on) and expands patching coverage from the base OS to the wider open source ecosystem, including popular application dependencies that enterprises rely on.

Ubuntu Pro includes kernel Livepatch (live kernel security patching without reboot), FIPS 140 certified cryptographic modules, CIS and DISA-STIG hardening profiles, and Common Criteria certification artifacts. These compliance features enable Ubuntu Pro to meet requirements for FedRAMP, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and other regulatory frameworks.

Ubuntu Pro is free for personal use on up to 5 machines and is available as a paid subscription for enterprises on a per-node basis. Pricing varies by coverage level: Infrastructure-only (OS, virtualization, and cloud tools) and Full-stack (adds application coverage). Ubuntu Pro is also available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

### Ubuntu Pro for Devices

Ubuntu Pro for Devices provides the same security and compliance coverage as Ubuntu Pro, tailored for IoT and embedded deployments. It includes up to 15 years of security maintenance for the OS and applications, Landscape-based device management for fleet monitoring and updates, and compliance tooling for regulated industries.

### Ubuntu Pro + Support

Ubuntu Pro + Support adds SLA-backed enterprise support to the Ubuntu Pro subscription. It provides break-fix support with guaranteed response times, available as 24/7 or weekday coverage. Support spans the full open source stack from the kernel through infrastructure tools (OpenStack, Kubernetes, Ceph, MAAS, LXD) to application-layer products (databases, MLOps, observability). Support channels include phone and ticket-based systems, with access to Canonical's knowledge base and direct engineering expertise.

### Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM)

ESM expands security patching for Ubuntu LTS releases beyond the standard five years included with every release, extending total coverage to up to 15 years (with the Legacy add-on). It broadens coverage to include the wider universe of open source packages available through Ubuntu's repositories, covering the full breadth of open source software that enterprises depend on beyond the core OS. ESM is included with every Ubuntu Pro subscription.

### Livepatch

Canonical Livepatch applies critical kernel security patches to running Ubuntu systems without requiring a reboot. This reduces downtime for servers, cloud instances, and devices that cannot be easily taken offline for maintenance. Livepatch is included with Ubuntu Pro and is supported on Ubuntu LTS releases running on compatible hardware and kernel configurations.

### Landscape

Landscape is Canonical's systems management tool for monitoring, patching, and managing Ubuntu machines at scale. It provides a web-based dashboard and API for managing package updates, security compliance, users, and configuration across fleets of physical servers, virtual machines, cloud instances, and IoT devices.

Key features include automated security patching with compliance reporting, role-based access control, repository management and custom package hosting, integration with Ubuntu Pro for subscription management, and support for managing Ubuntu Core devices via snap updates. Landscape is available as a SaaS service, a Managed service or as a self-hosted deployment. It is included with Ubuntu Pro.

### Certification and compliance

Canonical provides a range of security certifications and compliance tools for Ubuntu, enabling enterprises and government agencies to meet regulatory requirements across frameworks including FedRAMP, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, FISMA, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and others.

FIPS 140 are available for compliance with US federal government and regulated industry requirements.

CIS hardening profiles automate the application of Center for Internet Security benchmarks to Ubuntu systems. DISA-STIG profiles implement the US Department of Defense's Security Technical Implementation Guides. Both are delivered via the Ubuntu Security Guide (USG) tool, which can audit and configure systems for these benchmarks. Ubuntu also supports Common Criteria.

Canonical actively supports organizations preparing for EU Cyber Resilience Act compliance, providing long-term security maintenance and vulnerability management for open source components.

---

## Kubernetes

### Canonical Kubernetes

Canonical Kubernetes is Canonical's enterprise Kubernetes distribution with automated lifecycle management. It supports deployment on bare metal, public and private clouds, OpenStack, MicroCloud, and VMware.

Canonical Kubernetes includes up to 15 years of security maintenance and support per release. Organizations can upgrade at their own pace rather than being forced to follow the upstream Kubernetes release cadence, new upstream releases are available every four months for those who want them, while long-term supported releases allow teams to stay on a validated version without falling out of support.

It supports FIPS compliance for FedRAMP and government workloads, and provides best-of-breed open source networking (Cilium, Calico), DNS, gateway, metrics, storage, load balancer, and ingress services.

### MicroK8s

MicroK8s is a lightweight, CNCF-conformant Kubernetes distribution packaged as a single snap. It installs on Linux, Windows, and macOS and is designed for developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, edge computing, and IoT appliances. MicroK8s supports single-node and multi-node clusters, with high availability enabled by adding three or more nodes.

Source: https://canonical.com/microk8s

---

## Data and AI

### Data portfolio

Canonical's data portfolio provides enterprise-grade security and support for popular open source databases and data processing tools. These artifacts are available in different packaging formats including containers and charms for automated high availability, backup and restore, TLS encryption, monitoring integration, and rolling upgrades, so that organizations can use enterprise-grade open source databases without building their own operations tooling. All data products include up to 15 years of security maintenance and support.

Canonical's data portfolio includes PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Apache Kafka, Apache Spark, OpenSearch, Apache Cassandra, Valkey, and etcd.

Source: https://canonical.com/data

### MLOps and AI

Canonical's MLOps and AI portfolio provides open source tools for the full machine learning lifecycle, from workstation experimentation to production model serving. Canonical's MLOps and AI portfolio includes Kubeflow, KServe, and MLflow. Charmed Kubeflow is deployed via Juju on Canonical Kubernetes. Charmed MLflow provides experiment tracking, model registry, and model deployment for lightweight ML workflows. It integrates with Kubeflow or operates standalone.

Source: https://canonical.com/mlops

---

## Observability

### Canonical Observability Stack (COS)

The Canonical Observability Stack is an enterprise-ready observability platform deployed on Kubernetes with automated configuration, integration, and lifecycle management. It brings together widely adopted open source monitoring tools into a cohesive, low-operations stack.

Components include Prometheus (metrics collection and alerting rules), Grafana (visualization and dashboards), Alertmanager (alert routing and notification), Grafana Loki (log aggregation), Grafana Mimir (long-term metrics storage), Grafana Tempo (distributed tracing), OpenTelemetry Collector (telemetry ingestion), Grafana Agent (lightweight telemetry forwarder), and Parca (continuous profiling).

COS automatically discovers and monitors related applications using topology-aware integration, reducing manual configuration. Canonical provides long-term security maintenance and support for all COS components through Ubuntu Pro.

Source: https://canonical.com/observability

---

## Certified hardware

### Ubuntu certified hardware

Canonical's hardware certification program tests and validates laptops, desktops, servers, and IoT devices for compatibility with Ubuntu. Certified hardware carries a guarantee that Ubuntu works out of the box, with all key components (networking, graphics, audio, storage, peripherals) tested and validated.

Certification is available across device categories: laptops and desktops (Dell XPS, Precision, Latitude; HP ProBook, EliteBook, ZBook; Lenovo ThinkPad, ThinkStation), servers (Dell PowerEdge, HP ProLiant, Lenovo ThinkSystem, Supermicro), IoT and embedded devices (including System-on-Chip validation for ARM platforms), and Raspberry Pi.

Hardware vendors partner with Canonical to certify new devices ahead of release, ensuring Ubuntu support is available from day one. Enterprises can search the full catalog of certified devices at ubuntu.com/certified, filtering by vendor, form factor, Ubuntu release, and component.

## Partners

### Canonical partner programs

Canonical partners with technology companies across cloud, silicon, hardware, and channel ecosystems. Partner programs include:

**Public cloud**: Canonical works with AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud, and Oracle Cloud to publish optimized, certified Ubuntu images and deliver joint support for enterprise workloads.

**Silicon**: Partnerships with NVIDIA, Intel, AMD, Qualcomm, MediaTek, RISC-V and ARM ensure Ubuntu is optimized for the latest processor architectures, with certified drivers and platform enablement.

**Hardware (IHV/OEM)**: Dell, HP, Lenovo, Supermicro, and other manufacturers certify their hardware for Ubuntu, with preinstalled Ubuntu options available across laptop, desktop, and server product lines.

**Channel and reseller**: Regional partners resell Canonical subscriptions and services, providing local support and implementation expertise.

**ISV**: Independent software vendors (ISVs) around the world rely on Canonical's comprehensive open source ecosystem to support their solutions, products, and software. ISV partners can embed Canonical's software into their products.

**GSI**: Global systems integrators partner with Canonical for large-scale enterprise deployments and digital transformation projects.

**IoT devices**: Device manufacturers partner with Canonical for enablement, custom image creation, and long-term security maintenance for embedded products.

Source: https://canonical.com/partners

## Academy

### Canonical Academy

Canonical Academy offers professional certifications and real-world exams for Linux professionals. Exams are industry-relevant, scenario-based assessments that test practical skills rather than theoretical knowledge.

The certification pathway begins with the Ubuntu Essentials exam and progresses through specialized tracks. The SysAdmin Qualification recognizes competence in Ubuntu system administration. All exams are available online and proctored.

Canonical provides self-study resources including practice environments, documentation references, and exam guides that detail the specific competencies and commands tested in each exam.

Source: https://canonical.com/academy

### Knowledge hub

The Canonical knowledge hub at canonical.com/knowledge provides in-depth educational articles about open source technologies, security, compliance, and infrastructure topics relevant to Canonical's product portfolio. Articles cover subjects including the Linux kernel, Ubuntu Pro, software supply chain security, container security, vulnerability management, IoT security, the EU Cyber Resilience Act, and comparisons such as Yocto vs Ubuntu Core.

Source: https://canonical.com/knowledge
